candidates.attacker_control: The objectName path segment of GET/DELETE /api/buckets/{bucketName}/objects/{objectName} (and the objectName used by FileTransferApi.createTransfer). RouteContext.getRouteParam URL-decodes the segment (RouteContext.java:146-156), so encoded slashes (%2F) and dots (%2E) reach the API as '../../<file>' or '/absolute/path'; the BucketsApi comment on deleteObject ('will not parse ending / unless URI encoded') confirms encoded path characters are decoded and used.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: putObject (145-149) has a traversal guard, showing intent to block escapes on writes, but that guard is absent from the read/delete/find paths and is itself only a prefix check (canonicalPath.startsWith(root) without a separator boundary). uploadObject calls verifyObjectName, but getObject/deleteObject do not, and the regex permits '.' and '/', so it is not a traversal control. RdbBucket (RocksDB storage) is key/value based and unaffected; the issue is specific to FileSystemBucket, which is only selected when the bucket is filesystem-backed (confirmed in FileSystemBucketDatabase.getBucket and the example yamcs.yaml bucket path configurations). I found no later sanitization/normalization in the call chain, and no privilege check that compensates for the missing path containment.
candidates.impact: A user with read access to any filesystem-backed bucket (e.g. the bucket backing displays, which UI users normally can read) can read arbitrary files readable by the Yamcs process - /etc/passwd, etc/yamcs.yaml and security configuration, application.properties, truststore/keystore files, other instance data - and can trigger arbitrary file deletion with manage rights (Files.delete on a single file or empty directory). Because Path.resolve with an absolute argument discards the root entirely, plain absolute paths also work, not only '..' sequences.
candidates.prerequisites: The target bucket must be filesystem-backed: created via the 'buckets: - name/path' configuration (examples/cfdp, examples/simulation map 'displays', 'stacks', 'cfdpUp' to disk), or auto-discovered from directories under <dataDir>/<instance>/fsbuckets (FileSystemBucketDatabase.getBucket/listBuckets). The caller needs read or manage rights on that bucket (ReadBucket/ManageBucket on e.g. 'displays', or ManageAnyBucket; in the default security-disabled install the guest user is superuser; FileTransferApi.createTransfer additionally needs ControlFileTransfers). RocksDB-backed buckets (the default for yamcs createBucket) are not affected.
candidates.root_cause: Object names coming from HTTP requests are resolved directly into filesystem paths without containment validation. FileSystemBucket.putObject guards writes with a canonical-path prefix check (FileSystemBucket.java:145-149), but getObject (193-201), deleteObject (203-207) and findObject (209-218) do root.resolve(objectName) and then Files.readAllBytes / Files.delete / Files.readAttributes, so an object name containing '..' segments (or, because Path.resolve returns an absolute argument unchanged, an absolute path) escapes the bucket root. BucketsApi.getObject (138-162) and deleteObject (246-265) also never call the only name validator present (verifyObjectName, 327-334); only uploadObject does (181). Even verifyObjectName would not stop traversal, since OBJ_NAME_REGEXP (line 52) explicitly allows '.' and '/'.
candidates.title: Path traversal via unvalidated bucket object names in filesystem-backed storage (FileSystemBucket / BucketsApi)
candidates.trace: HTTP request -> HttpRequestHandler.route to ApiHandler -> BucketsApi.getObject:141 checkReadBucketPrivilege -> verifyAndGetBucket:144 -> YarchDatabaseInstance.getBucket:513 -> FileSystemBucketDatabase.getBucket:87 (root.resolve(bucketName), isDirectory) -> FileSystemBucket.findObject:211 root.resolve(objName) -> Files.exists/readAttributes -> FileSystemBucket.getObject:195-197 Files.readAllBytes(path). Same for deleteObject -> BucketsApi.deleteObject:255-259 -> FileSystemBucket.deleteObject:205-206 Files.delete(path). A second reachable sink is FileTransferApi.createTransfer (upload direction) -> CfdpService.startUpload:846 bucket.getObject(objectName), which reads the traversed file and pushes its contents over a configured CFDP entity (data exfiltration), with only checkReadBucketPrivilege on the bucket name.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Exploitability depends on a deployment having a filesystem-backed bucket reachable with the attacker's privileges; I could not run the server or confirm that the generated route for objectName accepts encoded slashes in every API version (the in-code TODO comment strongly implies it does). The exact upstream fix location (BucketsApi vs FileSystemBucket) is inferred, not observed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22: Path Traversal (arbitrary file read and deletion)

coverage_summary: Coverage was broad but not exhaustive. I searched the whole visible snapshot (2,394 files; no files excluded by the tool scope) for command execution, deserialization, XML/XXE parsing, SQL construction/execution, path/File/Path usage, template rendering, auth checks, privilege checks, and XSS sinks, then read the relevant parts of the HTTP stack (HttpRequestHandler, RouteHandler, RouteContext, ApiHandler, HttpServer, StaticFileHandler, AuthHandler, JwtHelper/TokenStore), the buckets/file-transfer stack (BucketsApi, FileSystemBucket/Database, RdbBucket/Database, FileTransferApi, FileSaveHandler, CfdpService), security code (SecurityStore, DirectoryAuthModule, YamlAuthModule, OpenIDAuthModule, PBKDF2PasswordHasher, SessionManager), IamApi/MdbApi/MdbOverrideApi/RocksDbApi/TableApi/InstancesApi, and the yamcs-web handlers/components (WebPlugin, WebFileDeployer, AngularHandler, Markdown, TimelineTooltip, AuthService). yamcs-xtce, simulator, packet-viewer, examples and large parts of yamcs-web component code were only spot-checked, not read end to end; no tests/CI runtime evidence was available in the snapshot.
limitations: Read-only static review; no server was run, so all exploitability statements are source-derived and unconfirmed.
The snapshot contains no test sources and only minimal docs, so intended behavior/regression tests could not be used to confirm or refute the candidate.

Generated protobuf route definitions are absent, so the exact route pattern for the objectName path parameter (single segment vs. catch-all) had to be inferred from client code and the in-file TODO comment.
Deployment-dependent preconditions (filesystem-backed bucket configured, effective bucket privileges) cannot be observed from source alone.
Several other plausible-but-weaker issues were rejected (see rejected leads); if the intended defect is one of those, this review would not cover it.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticFileHandler / AngularHandler absolute-path traversal: sanitizePath (StaticFileHandler.java:275-283) rejects '.'-segment forms but not absolute paths, and locateFile (99-107) uses staticRoot.resolve(path), which returns an absolute argument unchanged; a request target such as '/static//etc/passwd' or '//etc/passwd' (handled by the '*' Angular handler registered in WebPlugin.java:150) yields '/etc/passwd' after the prefix chop (getFilePath, 92-97) and would be served unauthenticated (requireAuth() false, 72-74). Source evidence is strong, but exploitability depends on double-slash request targets surviving to the handler and on yamcs-web being deployed; not selected because the bucket traversal has clearer data-flow evidence and a directly analogous guarded sibling method.
rejected_leads.reason: Strong but unconfirmed; selection preferred for the explicitly missing validation on object names.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflected XSS on the login page: authorize.html lines 48-52 render {{ request.client_id }}, {{ request.redirect_uri }} and {{ request.state }} from query/form parameters, while VarStatement.render (VarStatement.java:13-20) appends values with no HTML escaping and HandlerContext.render (HandlerContext.java:288-297) responds with text/html; /auth/authorize is unauthenticated (AuthHandler.requireAuth false).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible CWE-79, but the sink is a template resource plus a generic, deliberately non-escaping template engine, making the intended fix location and attacker impact less certain than the path traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: Unvalidated OAuth redirect_uri plus reusable authorization codes: AuthHandler.redirectWithCode (191-205) redirects to any request-supplied redirect_uri with the code, and handleTokenRequestWithAuthorizationCode (262-302) never invalidates codes (CODE_CACHE.getIfPresent) and does not authenticate the client, which could allow account takeover via an attacker-chosen redirect target.
rejected_leads.reason: Real design weakness (open redirect / code interception) but code is short-lived (60s) and the impact chain depends on user interaction; lower confidence that it is the reviewed defect.

rejected_leads.lead: Java deserialization of server-provided data in packet-viewer (PacketViewer.java:657 ObjectInputStream over getSerializedJavaDump) and of local cache in XtceDbFactory (XtceDbFactory.java:458).
rejected_leads.reason: The client trusts the server it connects to and the other path is local/admin-controlled, so the trust-boundary shift is weak.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL text injected from request into readRows via SqlBuilder.where(request.getQuery()) (TableApi.java:274-279); executeSql allows arbitrary StreamSQL with ControlArchiving (397-443).
rejected_leads.reason: readRows requires ReadTables and the custom StreamSQL engine offers little beyond filtered reads; executeSql already requires the archiving admin privilege, so impact/attacker model is weak.

rejected_leads.lead: Runtime algorithm text override via MdbOverrideApi.updateAlgorithm (MdbOverrideApi.java:144-189) executing server-side scripts.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the ChangeMissionDatabase system privilege, which is explicitly the privilege to define executable MDB content, so it is closer to intended capability than a boundary violation.

summary: Reviewed the assigned Yamcs 5.8.6 snapshot (2,394 visible files; mostly yamcs-core / yamcs-web / yamcs-xtce Java+TypeScript sources; tests and most docs are absent from the snapshot). I traced the main untrusted-input boundaries: the Netty HTTP stack and route transcoding, authentication (JWT/Basic/cookies, OAuth-ish login handler, sessions), the REST APIs for buckets, file transfers, tables and MDB, the CFDP file-transfer path, the filesystem-backed bucket implementation, the static-file handler, and the Angular web UI. The strongest source-supported issue is the path traversal in filesystem-backed buckets: HTTP-supplied object names reach FileSystemBucket.getObject/deleteObject/findObject, which resolve them against the bucket root (and, because Path.resolve honors absolute arguments, against any absolute path) without containment validation, while the analogous write path (putObject) does have such a check. Other plausible but weaker leads are noted as rejected. No code was executed; findings are source-evidence leads only.
